platforms.title: It's Not Just Salt — Licorice Tea Causes Swelling Too
platforms.meta_description: Puffy mornings and swollen legs by evening get blamed on salt alone — but licorice root has a documented, more surprising mechanism behind fluid retention.
platforms.body_html:
A puffy face in the morning and legs that feel heavy and swollen by evening usually get blamed on "too much salt yesterday," and sodium is a real driver — it pulls water into the space outside your cells through osmosis and stays there until the excess is cleared. But one of the most surprising contributors to fluid retention isn't salt at all. It's licorice.

Licorice Doesn't Just Add Sodium — It Changes Hormone Metabolism

Licorice root contains glycyrrhizin, a compound that blocks the enzyme (11β-HSD2) that normally breaks cortisol down in the kidneys. When that enzyme is blocked, cortisol keeps acting on receptors that drive the kidneys to hold onto sodium and water while flushing out potassium — a condition documented in the medical literature as licorice-induced pseudohyperaldosteronism. Case reports describe people who drank large amounts of licorice tea or ate licorice candy daily over months developing high blood pressure and dangerously low potassium levels as a result.

Instant ramen is a far more direct culprit. Sodium-content research on packaged noodles has found a single seasoning packet commonly contains 1,500 to 2,000 mg of sodium with almost no potassium to balance it, and the body holds onto water trying to dilute that sodium load back toward normal. Cheese compounds the problem two ways at once — sodium holds water in, while its saturated fat can sluggish circulation, so the swelling lingers longer than sodium alone would explain.

Prolonged sitting or standing adds another layer on top of diet, since gravity pulls fluid down into the legs when the calf muscles aren't moving enough to pump blood back toward the heart — which is part of why the same salty meal produces worse evening swelling on a day spent at a desk than a day spent walking around. Hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle can also make some people more prone to retaining fluid at certain times of the month, on top of whatever food triggers are in play, which is worth knowing so an unusually puffy week doesn't get blamed entirely on diet when the timing points elsewhere.

What Actually Brings the Swelling Down

  • Swap licorice tea for corn silk tea or another herbal option, and check ingredient labels on herbal remedies that may contain licorice root.
  • Leave the ramen broth instead of drinking it, and pair the noodles with potassium-rich foods like banana or potato.
  • Choose lower-sodium cheese and smaller portions rather than cutting it out completely.
  • Elevate your legs above heart level before bed — a simple habit that reliably reduces next-morning puffiness.

None of this means salt stops mattering — it's still the biggest lever for most people. It just means that if you're already watching sodium and still puffing up, the tea or supplement on your nightstand is worth a second look. If swelling is persistent, one-sided, or comes with shortness of breath, that pattern points toward something beyond diet and is worth a doctor's visit rather than dietary guesswork. This content is general health information, not a diagnosis.
